p85: 85.  It is true that, although they have the same content, the dictionaries are aimed at different audiences, since the second of them is entitled “Turkish Dictionary for Pupils”. It is clear that, in a dictionary intended for schoolchildren, greater care is required when giving the definitions of expressions which form part of everyday language but which might be perceived as humiliating or insulting. In the Court’s view, it would have been preferable to label such expressions as “pejorative” or “insulting”, rather than merely describing them as metaphorical. Such a precaution would have been in line with ECRI’s General Policy Recommendation No. 10, which provides that States should “promot[e] critical thinking among pupils and (...) equip[] them with the necessary skills to become aware of and react to stereotypes or intolerant elements contained in material they use” (see paragraph 39 above).
p86: 86.  However, the Court considers that this factor alone is not sufficient for it to substitute its own view for that of the domestic courts, particularly since the dictionary in question was not a school textbook and was neither distributed in schools nor recommended by the Ministry of Education as a reference book for school curricula (see paragraph 79 above).
p87: 87.  Lastly, the Court observes that the applicant’s case against the Language Association was examined by the domestic courts at two separate levels of jurisdiction (see paragraphs 31-34 above). It considers that, even though his claim was ultimately dismissed, the applicant had effective means of obtaining redress for his complaints, in accordance with Article 8 of the Convention.
p88: 88.  In the light of the foregoing, the Court considers that the domestic authorities did not overstep their margin of appreciation or disregard their positive obligation to secure to the applicant effective respect for his private life.
p89: 89.  There has accordingly been no violation of Article 8 of the Convention in respect of application no. 41029/04.
